title: Gödel Machine
subtitle: Self-referential, provably optimal self-improvement
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A 12-chapter course on the Gödel machine, Jürgen Schmidhuber's 2003 design for a self-referential, self-improving problem solver that rewrites its own code only after proving the rewrite helps. Based on the Wikipedia article, Schmidhuber's technical report, the Steunebrink and Schmidhuber paper on implementation and the Yudkowsky and Herreshoff work on the Löbian obstacle. Covers Gödel's ideas, the machine model, the axioms, the proof searcher, the target theorem, global optimality, bias-optimal proof search, examples, related work and limits, with Python labs on the built-in MicroPython engine. It is a theoretical design with no full implementation; speculative claims are marked as the author's own.

summary: A Gödel machine is a hypothetical self-improving computer program that aims to solve problems optimally. It rewrites its own code, but only when it can prove that the new code gives a better strategy.
Jürgen Schmidhuber proposed it in 2003, and it is named after Kurt Gödel, whose work inspired its mathematical foundations.

It belongs to meta-learning, or learning to learn. The motivation is that an ordinary program has one hardwired algorithm and does not account for a changing environment, whereas a Gödel machine can change its own algorithm, including the part that does the changing.
No full implementation has been created. The course treats it as a theory: you learn the machine step by step and build toy versions of its parts in Python.

A Gödel machine is a hypothetical self-improving computer program that aims to solve problems in an optimal way. It rewrites its own code when it can prove that the new code provides a better strategy.
It was invented by Jürgen Schmidhuber, first proposed in 2003, and is named after the logician Kurt Gödel, whose work inspired its mathematical foundations.

The idea sits within meta-learning, also called learning to learn. Proposed uses include automating human design decisions, transferring knowledge between related tasks, and designing more robust and general learning architectures.
The Wikipedia article is explicit that this is theory: no full implementation has been created.

Why is the design needed? A traditional computer solves a problem with one input and one output, and its initial algorithm is hardwired. That ignores a dynamic natural environment, where inputs keep arriving and the best behaviour changes. The Gödel machine was meant to overcome that.

The machine's name and power come from using provably useful changes of any part of its own code, in a self-referential way. Schmidhuber's paper calls it a class of mathematically rigorous, general, fully self-referential, self-improving problem solvers.
Those are the author's own claims; this course explains them and also covers the limits.

In outline, the machine starts with software that has three ingredients. An initial policy for dealing with the environment, which is allowed to be poor. A proof searcher, which hunts for formal proofs.
And an axiomatic description of itself and its world: its hardware, its goal, what is known about the environment, and what actions and computation cost.

The searcher looks for a proof of one special statement, called the target theorem. It says: rewriting myself in this particular way will give a higher expected utility than not rewriting. If a proof is found, the machine executes the rewrite.
The rewrite may change any part of the software, even the proof searcher itself.

The paper then argues that such a rewrite is globally optimal, not just locally. By then the machine has also had to prove that continuing to search for better rewrites is not worth waiting for. Chapter 7 covers this carefully.

Here is the machine's main loop, in words. Run the current policy and keep collecting reward. Meanwhile the proof searcher runs. When it proves a target theorem, switch to the proposed new code. Then carry on, with the new code now doing both the acting and the searching.

The route through the course follows the paper. Chapters 2 to 4 give the background and the machine model: Gödel's ideas, the state and the utility, and the axioms. Chapters 5 to 8 give the proof searcher, the target theorem, the optimality theorem and bias-optimal proof search.
The last chapters cover examples, related work, limits and a toy machine you build yourself.

A note on sources. They are the Wikipedia article on the Gödel machine, Schmidhuber's technical report on arXiv, the paper by Steunebrink and Schmidhuber on implementations, and the work of Yudkowsky and Herreshoff on the Löbian obstacle.

summary: Gödel showed in 1931 that any consistent formal system strong enough to express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. His proof encodes formulas as numbers, which lets a system talk about its own proofs and build a sentence that says it is not provable.
Related limits: a consistent system cannot prove its own consistency, and Rice's theorem says every non-trivial question about what a program computes is undecidable in general.
A Gödel machine reasons inside a formal system, so it inherits these limits. The paper accepts this: the machine ignores self-improvements whose usefulness it cannot prove.

items: Explain it simply. Gödel showed that any rule system strong enough for arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove. It is like a rulebook that cannot settle every question about itself. This sets the limits for self-checking machines.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does the incompleteness result say about proof?
The machine is named for Kurt Gödel because of how he turned logic on itself. In 1931 he introduced a way to encode formulas and proofs as natural numbers, now called Gödel numbering.
Once formulas are numbers, a statement about numbers can be a statement about formulas, so a system can talk about its own proofs.
With that, he built a sentence that says, in effect, I am not provable in this system. If the system is consistent, it cannot prove this sentence, yet the sentence is true.
That is the first incompleteness theorem: any formal system that encompasses arithmetic is either flawed, meaning inconsistent, or contains statements that it cannot prove.
Schmidhuber describes Gödel as the founder of theoretical computer science, because he introduced a universal coding language based on integers.
The Gödel machine reuses that trick in a practical direction: its software and its proofs are strings, and the axioms include a description of its own code.

lesson.tex: \text{Gödel number of } s_1 s_2 \dots s_n \;=\; 2^{c(s_1)} \cdot 3^{c(s_2)} \cdots p_n^{\,c(s_n)}

items: Here is a simple version of numbering, with my own symbol codes. Give each symbol a positive code c. Then raise the first prime, 2, to the code of the first symbol, the second prime, 3, to the code of the second symbol, and so on, and multiply.
Unique factorization into primes means the number can be decoded back into the symbols.
A second famous limit: a consistent system cannot prove its own consistency. Later chapters connect this to Löb's theorem and to a problem that arises when an agent must trust its own proofs.

A third limit comes from computability. Rice's theorem says that any non-trivial property of what a program computes is undecidable in general. So no algorithm can decide, for every program, whether it is better than another.
A system that must prove such properties will be able to prove only some of them.

What does this mean for a Gödel machine? The wiki article states it directly: even a Gödel machine with unlimited computational resources must ignore those self-improvements whose effectiveness it cannot prove.
The paper adds a point about resources: a machine with limited time and space cannot profit from improvements it cannot prove within its limits.

The paper also notes that the machine does not exceed ordinary computers in power. In an interview Schmidhuber says it is not computationally more powerful than a Turing machine. Its claim is about efficiency: it can exploit any provably useful speed-up of any part of its software.
The practice section has a numbering lab: you encode a symbol list as a Gödel number and decode it back. Keep to short lists, since the numbers grow very fast.

practice.intro: Give each symbol a positive integer code. Write godel_number(codes): the product of the n-th prime raised to the n-th code (primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...). The empty list gives 1. Keep inputs short: the numbers get large quickly.

practice.title: Decode a Gödel number
practice.intro: Write decode_godel(n): the inverse of the numbering. Divide n by 2 as many times as possible and count, then by 3, and so on, until n is 1. Return the list of exponents. Assume every code is at least 1, so there are no gaps.
practice.hint: Loop over primes. For each prime count how many times it divides n.
practice.solution:
def decode_godel(n):
    primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]
    out = []
    i = 0
    while n > 1:
        count = 0
        while n % primes[i] == 0:
            n = n // primes[i]
            count += 1
        out.append(count)
        i += 1
    return out

summary: The machine's hardware has a single life made of discrete cycles t = 1, 2, ..., T. The state s(t) changes by a hardwired transition function that depends on the previous state and the environment.

Four variables matter: time holds the binary encoding of t; x holds the environment's input; y holds the machine's output; and p is the software, which at the start contains an initial policy and an initial proof searcher.

The goal is to maximize expected utility: the conditional expectation of the sum of future rewards from now until the end of life, under an unknown environment distribution drawn from a set of possible ones.

items: Explain it simply. The machine has a state, a way to act and a score for how well it is doing. Utility is that score added up over its whole life. Everything it does is judged by it.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does the utility function add up?

To define the machine precisely, Schmidhuber's report starts with the hardware. It has a single life, which consists of discrete cycles or time steps t = 1, 2, and so on up to T. The final time T may or may not be known in advance.
The hardware can be a universal Turing machine, a space-bounded Turing machine or the abstract model of a personal computer. At any moment it has a state s(t), a finite binary string.
The state changes by a hardwired state transition function F, which takes the previous state and the environment's reaction and returns the new state.

Four variables are stored in the state. Time holds a binary encoding of the current step, starting from 1 and increasing every cycle. The variable x holds input from the environment; it changes only when a program executes an instruction that requests input.
The variable y holds the outputs; its default value at the start is zero. And p is the software, which includes an initial policy for interacting with the environment, plus an initial proof searcher.

The goal. At every time the machine tries to maximize its expected future success. The paper formalizes this as the utility u of the current state and environment: the conditional expectation of the sum of all rewards from the present time up to the end of life.

In this formula r of tau is the real-valued reward encoded in the state at step tau. The expectation uses a distribution mu, which is unknown. It is drawn from a set M of distributions that could describe the environment. The variable time is the current time, taken from the state s.

This formulation allows alternatives. A designer could use worst-case performance over M instead of the expectation, or reward per time interval. The Wikipedia article adds that the utility accounts for the possibility of extending the machine's expected lifespan.

An important consequence: since the utility function is stored in the machine's state, the machine can reason about it, and may in principle change it. But a change of the utility function is allowed only if the new one is provably better according to the present utility function.
This is the reply to the worry that the machine might adopt a bogus goal.
The practice section computes expected utility over a few environment distributions and the cumulative reward between two times.

summary: The machine's initial software includes an axiomatic description of itself and its world. The proof searcher derives theorems from these axioms by inference rules.

The axiom groups are hardware axioms, reward axioms, environment axioms, uncertainty and string-manipulation axioms, initial-state axioms and utility axioms. Together they let the machine prove statements about its own future states and rewards.
Because the axiom system is part of the software, it can itself be rewritten, but only by a proven-useful rewrite. Optimality claims hold relative to a consistent axiom system.

items: Explain it simply. The axioms are the starting facts the machine is allowed to trust: how its hardware works, what its program does and what the score means. Proofs are built only from these.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what kinds of facts sit in the axiom set?

The machine's initial software p(1) carries an axiomatic system A. The proof searcher derives theorems from A with a few inference rules, and a theorem of the right form triggers a rewrite. The paper lists what A contains.

Hardware axioms describe how the state can change from one cycle to the next. For a Turing machine they cover the tape contents, the head positions and the internal state. For a microprocessor they cover registers and instruction pointers.
With these the machine can derive what its hardware will do if it runs a given program.

Reward axioms describe the costs of hardware instructions and the physical costs of output actions. They also describe reward events arriving in the input, and the total lifetime as a scalar. A typical derived quantity is R of t1 and t2, the cumulative reward between two times.

Environment axioms restrict how new inputs are produced, given earlier inputs and outputs. They can be very weak, for example saying the true distribution is any computable one, or the Speed Prior. They can be strong, for example a Markovian interface or a fully predictable environment.

Uncertainty axioms and string-manipulation axioms are the standard axioms of arithmetic, calculus, probability theory, statistics and string manipulation. They allow proofs about future values of variables, expected rewards and remaining lifetime.
This is why the framework can handle uncertainty with ordinary formal mathematics.

Initial-state axioms are statements about the contents of the state at time 1, for instance that a particular substring of the state equals a particular string. They let the machine reconstruct its own initial code, which is needed to talk about itself.
Utility axioms define the goal: the utility function u, for example the expected sum of future rewards. Because the utility is an axiom, a target theorem can compare utilities of different futures.

Now two cautions. First, consistency. The optimality theorem in chapter 7 assumes the axiom system is consistent. If it were inconsistent, it could prove anything, including target theorems for harmful rewrites.

Second, the system is not fixed: since the axioms are part of the software, a proven rewrite may add theorems derived from the axioms, or replace axioms, as the paper lists among possible self-improvements.
The practice section lets you classify statements by axiom group and use the standard result that makes hardware axioms useful: simulate a tiny machine's state transitions.

summary: The proof searcher does not enumerate proofs by brute force, which would take time exponential in the proof size. It tests proof techniques: programs, written in a universal language, whose output is a proof.

A proof technique can modify the proof only through six instructions: get-axiom, apply-rule, delete-theorem, set-switchprog, check and state2theorem. Since there is no other way to change the proof, an incorrect theorem can never be inserted, which makes verifying a proof trivial.
A proof is a list of theorems. Each theorem is either an axiom or follows from earlier theorems by an inference rule, such as modus ponens.

glossary.def: A program, in a universal language, that outputs a proof by calling the proof-modifying instructions.
Appends the n-th axiom of the axiom scheme to the proof.
Applies the k-th inference rule to the m-th and n-th theorems and appends the result.
Removes a theorem to free storage; it can no longer be used.
Sets the candidate rewrite to a substring of the proof technique's scratch memory.
Tests whether the last theorem is a target theorem and, if so, arranges the switch.
Turns a currently observable part of the state into a time-stamped theorem.

Verification is therefore trivial.

items: Explain it simply. The proof searcher is a worker that tries to build proofs by chaining the axioms, one allowed step at a time. Like a clerk trying many arguments until one fits the form.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does the searcher do with the time it is given?

The proof searcher is the part of the initial software that hunts for a proof of the target theorem. The simplest way to search for proofs is brute force: enumerate all proofs in order of size. That takes exponential time in the proof size, so it is hopeless for anything but tiny proofs.

The paper instead lets the searcher test proof techniques. A proof technique is a program, written in a universal language such as a variant of PROLOG or a FORTH-like language, whose output is a proof.

Techniques can read parts of the machine's state, including the input x and the code of the initial software, and they write temporary results to a scratch area. Their output goes into a string variable called proof.

A proof technique may change the proof only through six instructions. Because these are the only ways to modify the proof, it is impossible to insert an incorrect theorem, so checking that a proof is valid is trivial. The six are as follows.

One, get-axiom with an index n: it appends the n-th axiom from the axiom scheme to the proof. Two, apply-rule with k, m and n: it applies the k-th inference rule, for example modus ponens, to the m-th and n-th theorems, and appends the result.
If the rule does not apply, the current proof technique is interrupted.

Three, delete-theorem with m: it removes the m-th theorem, which frees storage; deleted theorems can no longer be used. Four, set-switchprog with m and n: it sets the candidate rewrite, the switchprog, to the substring of the scratch area from m to n, provided that substring is not empty.

Five, check: it tests whether the last theorem is a target theorem. If it is, and there is still enough time to set the switch bit before the deadline, it sets the bit, waits, and transfers control to the switchprog.

Six, state2theorem with m and n: it converts the currently observable contents of part of the state into a time-stamped theorem. Observed facts need no proof, because the observation has already happened.

Let us see a tiny version. Suppose the axioms are p, p implies q, and q implies r. A proof technique runs: get-axiom 1, get-axiom 2, apply modus ponens to theorems 1 and 2, which gives q. Then get-axiom 3 and apply modus ponens again to get r.
Every line is either an axiom or a valid consequence, so the final proof is correct by construction.

The searcher is an online variant of universal search. It tests techniques one after another, giving each a budget of steps, and undoes their effects on the scratch area between tests. Chapter 8 covers the exact scheme and why it is asymptotically optimal.
In the practice section you implement the proof builder with get-axiom, modus ponens and delete-theorem, and see that an invalid step is rejected, so no wrong theorem ever enters.

summary: A switchprog is a candidate program that can rewrite any part of the machine's software. The machine runs it only if it has proved a target theorem: the utility with the switch bit set to 1 is higher than with the bit set to 0.

Setting the bit to 0 means continuing as before, with the searcher still looking for other rewrites. Setting it to 1 means running the switchprog at time t1. The time t1 accounts for the delay between finding the proof and acting on it.
A relaxed version replaces the strict inequality with at least as high, so the machine rewrites itself as soon as the change is provably not harmful.

items: Explain it simply. The target theorem says: if I switch to this new program now, my total future score will be higher. Only when the machine proves that does it switch.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what exactly must the target theorem state?

When a proof technique calls set-switchprog, it names a substring of its scratch area as the candidate rewrite. That candidate is the switchprog. It is a program that, when run, may rewrite any part of the machine's software p, including the axioms, the policy and the proof searcher itself.

The machine will run the switchprog only if it has proved that doing so is better than not doing so. The statement to prove is called the target theorem. To state it, the machine uses a switch bit. When the bit is 0, the machine continues as before.
When it is 1, the machine runs the switchprog at a time t1.

Read this as: the utility of the world in which the switch bit is one is higher than the utility of the world in which it is zero. The symbol with the circled plus means replace the switch bit value in the state. The time t1 handles the delay between finding a proof and acting on it.

The check instruction, from the previous chapter, does the rest. It looks at the last theorem. If that is a target theorem, it checks that there is still time to set the bit before t1. If so it sets the bit, waits until t1 passes, and transfers control to the switchprog.

Importantly, the continue-as-before option is not the same as doing nothing. Continuing as before means the proof searcher keeps looking for other rewrites. So the target theorem effectively says that the switchprog is better than waiting for any later rewrite the searcher might find.
Chapter 7 uses exactly this point to explain global optimality.

The proof does not need exact numbers. The paper stresses that the machine only has to show which of the two utilities is higher, not to compute them. For example, a factor-2 speed-up of a proof-searcher subroutine can be shown worthwhile without knowing the exact utility.

The relaxed version. Replace the strict greater-than with at-least-as-high. Then the machine rewrites itself as soon as it can prove the change will not make things worse, and the optimality theorem holds with the weaker inequality.

Here is a worked example with numbers. The current policy earns 10 reward per step, and 100 steps remain. A switchprog gives 12 per step but needs 5 steps to run, during which nothing is earned. Continuing earns 1000. Switching earns 12 times 95, which is 1140. So the target theorem is true.
If instead the switch took 20 steps, switching would earn 12 times 80, which is 960, so it is false.
In the practice section you check target theorems for numbers like these, order the steps of a switch, and use the Switch Explorer app.

summary: Theorem 4.1 in the paper says that once the machine has proved a target theorem and switched, the resulting change is globally optimal: no other self-rewrite, now or later, could have done better, given the axioms.
The reason is that the continue option already includes every future rewrite the searcher might find.

So the machine is not greedy. It does not take the first improvement; it takes a switch only when the proof says that switching now beats everything it could do by waiting. The paper also argues that all meta-levels collapse into one, because the same proof searcher improves itself.
The guarantee is relative to the axioms and requires them to be consistent. It is not a guarantee about the real world beyond what the axioms say.

glossary.def: No other rewrite, available now or later, would have a higher expected utility, according to the axioms.
Taking the first improvement found, without comparing with future improvements.
A level of learning that improves a lower level, such as a learner that improves the learner.

items: Explain it simply. Global optimality means any self-change that is provably good will be found, but no change is made unless it is provably worth it. The machine never takes a step it cannot justify.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why is each accepted rewrite safe, given the axioms?

Chapter 6 ended with a subtle point: the target theorem compares switching with continuing, and continuing includes the possibility that the proof searcher finds something even better later. This chapter spells out what follows from it.

Theorem 4.1 in the paper reads, in plain words: given the initial axiom system, once the machine has executed a rewrite after proving a target theorem, no other rewrite, whether at that moment or at any later moment, can have higher expected utility. The proof is short.
At the time of the switch the machine has proved that u with the switch is greater than u without it. The without-it branch contains every future rewrite. So no future rewrite beats this switch.

That makes the machine non-greedy. A greedy learner takes any improvement it can find. The Gödel machine may instead decline an improvement now, because it can prove that waiting for a better one pays off more, for example a rewrite that makes the proof searcher itself faster.
The comparison is not with the present policy; it is with the best future.

Take a small example with numbers. Policy A earns 10 per step. Candidate B earns 12 per step but costs 30 steps to apply. Candidate C earns 20 per step but costs 40 steps to apply, and it is provable only later.
With 100 steps left, B gives 12 times 70, which is 840, against 1000 for staying, so B is not worth it. A greedy rule that only checks rate would jump to B and lose.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} u_{\text{switch}} \;=\; r_{\text{new}}\,(T - t_1 - c) \\[0.6em] u_{\text{stay}} \;=\; r_{\text{old}}\,(T - t_1) \end{gathered}

items: The paper also discusses the relaxed target theorem, with at-least-as-high in place of strictly higher, and shows that global optimality still holds in the sense that no later rewrite can be strictly better. The strict version avoids pointless rewrites with equal utility.

The collapse of meta-levels. In many learning systems you stack levels: a learner, a meta-learner that tunes the learner, a meta-meta-learner, and so on, each fixed by the designer. Here the proof searcher can rewrite the entire software, including itself, so there is a single level.
Improvements to improvement happen inside the same loop and are judged by the same target theorem.

The paper answers common worries in a short question and answer section. What if a later self-change breaks the machine? Any change was proved to raise utility before it was executed, so a later change is judged the same way.
What if the machine adopts a bogus utility? A new utility is acceptable only if the present utility says it is better, so a reward-hacking replacement would fail the test.

Be careful about what is claimed. These are mathematical results inside a formal framework, and they inherit its assumptions: a consistent axiom system, a correct hardware model, and enough resources to find proofs. Whether a real machine could ever satisfy them is open, as chapter 11 discusses.
In the practice section you compute the total reward of a plan with several switches, and find the best single switch, which shows why comparing with the stay option matters.

practice.title: Total reward with switches
practice.intro: The machine earns rate0 per step for horizon steps. A switch is [time, new_rate, cost]: at that time it spends cost steps earning nothing, then continues at new_rate. Write total_reward(rate0, horizon, switches) for switches sorted by time. Steps are numbered from 0 to horizon-1. Ignore any switch whose time is at or after the horizon, and cut off a switch cost that runs past the end.
practice.hint: Accumulate reward up to each switch, jump over the cost steps, then change the rate.
practice.solution:
def total_reward(rate0, horizon, switches):
    t = 0
    rate = rate0
    total = 0
    for sw in switches:
        when = sw[0]
        if when >= horizon:
            break
        total += (when - t) * rate
        t = when
        t = min(horizon, t + sw[2])
        rate = sw[1]
    total += (horizon - t) * rate
    return total

summary: Bias-optimal proof search, or BIOPS, is the paper's search scheme for the proof searcher. It tests proof techniques in phases: in phase i, each technique w with probability P(w) of at least 2 to the minus i receives a budget of 2 to the i times P(w) steps.

Theorem 5.1 says that if a proof technique exists that proves the target theorem in time t, BIOPS finds it in time of order t divided by P(w), up to a constant factor. Bias-optimal means optimal given the bias, which is the probability distribution P over techniques.

BIOPS is an online search. When a technique fails, the effects on the scratch memory are undone, and the next one runs. A successful technique may be reused: the Optimal Ordered Problem Solver shares this idea.

glossary.def: Levin's scheme for searching programs in order, giving each a time share proportional to its prior probability.
The probability of technique w, often 2 to the minus its code length.
One round of the search; phase i doubles the total time of the previous phase.
The prior distribution over techniques, which says which are tried first.
Within a constant factor of the best possible, given the bias.
Bias-optimal proof search, Schmidhuber's scheme for the Gödel machine's searcher.
Optimal Ordered Problem Solver, a related method that reuses earlier solutions.

keyPoints: BIOPS runs in phases i = 1, 2, 3, ...

items: Explain it simply. BIOPS shares search time fairly among all candidate proofs, favouring short ones. Like a library clerk who tries every request, giving shorter books quicker attention.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how does time get shared among proof attempts?

The proof searcher needs a schedule for trying proof techniques. Chapter 5 said the simplest way, enumerating all proofs by size, is exponential. Universal search, invented by Leonid Levin, does better: it tries programs in a way that spends time in proportion to their probability.

Say each proof technique w has a probability P of w. A natural choice is 2 to the minus the length of its code, so shorter techniques are more likely. The schedule works in phases. In phase i, every technique with P of w at least 2 to the minus i is run for 2 to the i times P of w steps.

Consider the total time. In phase i the budgets add up to at most 2 to the i times the sum of the probabilities, which is at most 2 to the i. Each phase costs at most twice the previous one, so the search time is dominated by the last phase.

Now the guarantee. Suppose technique w proves the target theorem in t steps. It first gets a large enough budget in the phase where 2 to the i times P of w is at least t. That phase i satisfies 2 to the i of order t divided by P of w. All phases up to i together take at most about twice that.
So BIOPS finds the proof in time of order t over P of w. This is Theorem 5.1.

This is what bias-optimal means. BIOPS is not faster than a perfect searcher, but it is within a constant factor of the best searcher that uses the same bias. It cannot avoid the constant, which is large when the winning technique is improbable, that is, long.

The paper also defines n-bias-optimal variants, in which the search is allowed to be a factor n slower in exchange for other properties, and notes that a proof technique's effects are undone before the next one starts, so each test is independent.

Relation to OOPS. The Optimal Ordered Problem Solver, also by Schmidhuber, applies the same time allocation to a sequence of tasks and lets later tasks reuse the code that solved earlier ones. The paper suggests the Gödel machine's searcher can profit from this by keeping useful proof fragments.
In the practice section you implement a small Levin-style search. Each technique has a code length k, so P is 2 to the minus k, and a step count needed to succeed or minus one if it never succeeds.

summary: The paper lists several kinds of self-improvement the machine could prove useful, from small speed-ups of a subroutine to replacing the utility function or the axioms themselves. Each kind needs a proof inside the axiom system.

Three illustrative scenarios appear in the paper: a program that speeds up a graph or travelling-salesman solver, a search for a counterexample to Goldbach's conjecture, and a robot with limited fuel that must plan around depots under a weak environment assumption, the Speed Prior.
These are thought experiments, not experimental results. They show how a target theorem could be stated and what must be proved.

items: Explain it simply. Examples include rewriting a slow routine to be faster or changing the search itself. The machine can improve even the part that finds improvements.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: which part of itself can the machine improve?
What can a Gödel machine improve? In section 6.1 the paper lists several kinds of self-improvement, all of them proved useful by the target theorem.

They include: changing the initial policy; speeding up a subroutine, which gives more reward or more search per step; changing the proof searcher or its search order; adding axioms or lemmas that shorten future proofs; modifying the hardware model after the real hardware changes; and, in principle, changing the utility function or the axioms themselves.

A key point is that a speed-up of the proof searcher is a self-improvement like any other. A faster searcher finds later proofs sooner, and this can be proved worthwhile even without knowing the exact utility, as chapter 6 noted. This is how the machine's efficiency can compound.
Example one: a graph or travelling-salesman solver. Suppose the policy is a slow heuristic. A rewrite replaces it with a faster algorithm.

The machine proves from the hardware axioms that the new code runs in fewer steps and returns the same answer, and from the utility axioms that finishing earlier gives more reward. That proves the target theorem.

Example two: Goldbach's conjecture. Suppose the machine's task is to find a counterexample. The policy checks even numbers in turn. If a counterexample exists, the reward comes when it is found, so a faster check is useful.
If none exists the policy runs forever and the reward never arrives, so the machine should not spend unlimited resources on it. The paper uses this to show how time budgeting matters.

Here is the check itself. For an even number n, look for a prime p up to n over 2 such that n minus p is also prime. If you find one, n is fine. If you reach no such p, n is a counterexample. The practice section implements this for small numbers.
No counterexample is known to exist; it has been checked far beyond what the lab will do.

Example three: a fuel robot. A robot uses one liter of fuel per hour and must keep running to earn reward. The environment contains fuel depots at certain times, but the robot does not know the true environment.

The paper uses the Speed Prior as a weak assumption: the environment is computable, and fast-computable environments are more likely. The machine can then prove statements about expected survival under that prior.

The point of all three: a self-improvement is justified by a proof about future reward, and the proof depends on the axioms. The more precise the axioms, the more improvements the machine can justify. The weaker the axioms, the fewer.
In the practice section you search for Goldbach pairs, scan for a counterexample below a limit, and compute how long a robot survives.

summary: The Gödel machine is compared with several earlier ideas. Hutter's AIXI is a theoretically optimal agent that combines Solomonoff's universal prediction with expectimax planning, but it is incomputable. A resource-bounded variant, AIXI(t,l), is computable but still has a huge constant.
Hutter's HSEARCH is a hardwired proof searcher whose search is bias-optimal but cannot be rewritten.
The Gödel machine differs in that its proof searcher can rewrite itself. Related Schmidhuber methods include OOPS, the Success-Story Algorithm for evaluating self-modifications, and Universal Search.
The differences are about what is fixed and what can change, so a table of what is hardwired in each approach is a good way to remember them.

glossary.def: Hutter's theoretically optimal reinforcement learning agent: Solomonoff induction plus expectimax. Incomputable.
A computable, resource-bounded variant of AIXI with time t and length l, with a very large constant factor.
Hutter's hardwired search for proofs of program properties, bias-optimal but not self-modifying.
A universal prediction method that weights every computable hypothesis by 2 to the minus its length.
A planning rule: maximize over actions, average over chance outcomes.
A method that keeps a self-modification only if reward rate improved since it was made.
The Levin complexity: program length plus the log of its running time.

keyPoints: AIXI is optimal but incomputable; AIXI(t,l) is computable but impractical.
HSEARCH uses a fixed bias-optimal proof search; the Gödel machine can rewrite its search.

Each approach differs in what is fixed.

items: Explain it simply. The idea sits next to evolution, meta-learning and universal search. They all try to improve the improver, but differ in how much they trust proof over trial.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what separates proof-based from trial-based self-improvement?

The Gödel machine did not appear in a vacuum. The paper compares it with several lines of work. The most important comparison is with Marcus Hutter's AIXI, which was published at around the same time.

AIXI combines two ideas. Solomonoff induction predicts the future by giving every computable hypothesis a weight of 2 to the minus its length. Expectimax planning then picks, at each step, the action that maximizes expected reward over the predicted futures.
The result is optimal in a certain sense for a wide class of environments, but it is incomputable.

Hutter also gave AIXI(t,l), a computable variant that considers only policies of length at most l and runs each for at most t steps. It is asymptotically optimal in some sense, but the constant is enormous, so it is not practical.
Hutter's HSEARCH searches for proofs that a program is optimal, using a fixed bias-optimal scheme.

The paper's comparison, in short. AIXI(t,l) and HSEARCH have hardwired searchers and do not improve themselves. The Gödel machine's searcher, which is also a bias-optimal proof searcher, can be rewritten by a proven-useful switch, so it can overcome the initial constants over time.
That is the claim; it has not been shown in practice.

Related Schmidhuber methods. The Optimal Ordered Problem Solver, OOPS, solves a sequence of problems and keeps useful earlier programs for reuse. The Success-Story Algorithm, SSA, lets a learner modify itself and keeps a modification only if the reward rate since it was made beats the rate before.
SSA checks success empirically, whereas the Gödel machine checks by proof.

Universal Search by Levin, chapter 8, is the root of the time-allocation idea. A related quantity is Levin complexity, Kt: the length of a program plus the logarithm of its running time. It trades off short code against slow code, and it is the quantity that universal search implicitly minimizes.

The Speed Prior, also by Schmidhuber, is a prior on environments that favours those computable quickly. It is a weaker, more realistic assumption than the Solomonoff prior, and it appears in the fuel robot example.
Note the difference between approaches in kind. AIXI is a mathematical definition of an optimal agent. The Gödel machine is a design for an agent that improves itself by proof.
They are not competing implementations; they answer different questions, and the paper explicitly discusses how its machine could use AIXI-like components.

summary: The Gödel machine remains a theoretical design. Resource limits mean it can prove only improvements whose proofs fit in time and space; by Rice's theorem it must ignore many useful changes; and by Blum's speed-up theorem some problems have no optimal program at all.

Löb's theorem, a relative of Gödel's second incompleteness theorem, creates the Löbian obstacle: an agent that trusts its own proofs seems to run into a barrier when it tries to prove that a successor which uses the same reasoning is safe.
Yudkowsky and Herreshoff studied this in the context of self-modifying systems.

Steunebrink and Schmidhuber explored what an implementation would need, such as a solver and searcher pair and meta-circular evaluators. Claims about consciousness or about humans being Gödel machines are speculation by the author and are not results.

items: Explain it simply. Critics say proofs may take forever, axioms may be wrong, and the utility may not capture what we want. A careful machine is only as good as its assumptions.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what are two practical obstacles to building one?

This chapter collects the limits, in the spirit of reading the paper with a critical eye. The first is the simplest: there is no complete implementation. The design is mathematically precise, but running it needs a lot of engineering that nobody has shown to work.

Second, resources. The paper admits that a machine with limited time and space cannot profit from improvements whose proofs are too long. It also admits that by Rice's theorem many useful improvements are undecidable.
Even with unlimited resources, the machine must ignore those self-improvements whose effectiveness it cannot prove.

Third, the Blum speed-up theorem. Manuel Blum showed that there are computable problems for which every program has a much faster one, so there is no optimal program. The paper notes that for such problems no solver can be best, and a Gödel machine can only keep speeding up.

Fourth, the Löbian obstacle. Löb's theorem says that if a system proves that provability of a statement implies the statement, then it proves the statement. As a result a consistent system cannot assert that its own proofs are sound.
For a self-modifying agent that approves a successor only when it can prove the successor safe, this blocks a naive proof that a successor with the same reasoning is safe.

Yudkowsky and Herreshoff's work at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute discusses this obstacle in detail and explores partial ways around it. Their conclusion is that tiling, an agent trusting a successor of its own kind, is hard under the straightforward proof-based approach.
This is a research problem, not a refutation: the Gödel machine's target theorem asks about utility, not trust in the successor's proofs, and it is not settled how the two connect.

Fifth, the question of implementation. Steunebrink and Schmidhuber's paper on Gödel machine implementations describes an architecture with a Solver, which acts in the environment, and a Searcher, which looks for proofs, using meta-circular evaluators so that the system can interpret and modify its own code. They also describe a system called Sleight. Their work shows how much is needed beyond the original mathematical description.

Finally, a word on speculation. Schmidhuber has suggested connections between the Gödel machine and consciousness, and has suggested that humans may be Gödel machines in a loose sense. These are the author's own views; they are not derived from the theorems and are not established.
The course marks them as speculative, and so should anyone who cites them.

The practical lesson is to read the guarantees carefully. They say: given consistent axioms, correct hardware and enough time, each executed rewrite is globally optimal. They do not say that a real system exists, that the axioms are right, or that proofs will be found in time.
In the practice section you simulate a resource-bounded machine that can use only provable rewrites that fit in a proof budget, which shows what the ignore-the-unprovable rule means in practice.

summary: The capstone is a toy model that keeps the essential logic: the machine earns reward at a rate, searches for proofs about candidate rewrites, and switches only when the proved total reward is strictly higher than staying.

Each candidate has a new rate, a switching cost and a proof time. Searching takes part of the machine's effort, modelled by a share. The toy leaves out real logic: the proofs are replaced by arithmetic.
Building it ties the earlier chapters together: the target theorem is the comparison, the proof time is the delay, and the order of candidates is the search order.

items: Explain it simply. The toy machine has a tiny set of facts and a simple checker, so you can watch it prove, switch and keep going. Small enough to see every step.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what is the condition for the toy to switch programs?

Now put it together. The toy machine has an integer reward rate and a horizon, the number of steps in its life. It also has a list of candidate rewrites. Each candidate has a name, a new rate, a switching cost in steps, and a proof time, the number of steps its proof search needs.

The machine works through the candidates in order. For each one it spends the proof time searching. During the search it still acts, but a share of its effort goes to searching, so the reward is reduced to the rate times 100 minus the share, divided by 100, using integer division.

When the proof is done, the machine compares two totals for the remaining time. Staying earns the remaining steps at the current rate, with the share applied. Switching loses the cost steps, then earns the rest at the new rate, with the share applied.
If switching is strictly greater, the machine switches: it spends the cost steps, sets the new rate and records the candidate's name.

A candidate is skipped when its proof time would not finish before the end: if the current time plus the proof time is at least the horizon, the machine stops searching and just earns until the end. A rejected candidate still costs its proof time, as in a real search.

At the end, add the reward from the current time to the horizon at the current rate. Return the total and the names of the candidates that were switched to, in order. This function is the capstone lab.

Try it with numbers. Rate 10, horizon 100, share 0. Candidate A: new rate 14, cost 5, proof time 10. After 10 steps, t is 10 and total 100. Remaining 90. Stay: 900. Switch: 85 times 14 which is 1190. Switch, t becomes 15, rate 14. Then 85 steps at 14 add 1190. The total is 1290.

Compare with the theory. The toy keeps three properties: a rewrite happens only when the comparison says it is strictly better, comparison is with staying for the rest of the time, and time spent searching is paid for.
It omits the axioms, the logic, the self-reference and the rewriting of the searcher. So it illustrates the decision rule, not the machine.

practice.title: The toy Gödel machine
practice.intro: Write toy_godel(rate0, horizon, candidates, share). Start with t = 0, total = 0, rate = rate0, and an empty list of switched names. For each candidate [name, new_rate, cost, proof_time] in order: if t + proof_time >= horizon, stop. Otherwise add the reward for proof_time steps at the current rate, namely proof_time * rate * (100 - share) // 100, and move t forward by proof_time. Let remaining = horizon - t. stay = remaining * rate * (100 - share) // 100. switch = (remaining - cost) * new_rate * (100 - share) // 100, but never below 0 (if remaining < cost use 0). If switch > stay, then t += cost, rate = new_rate, and append the name (the cost steps earn nothing). At the end add (horizon - t) * rate * (100 - share) // 100. Return [total, switched_names].
practice.hint: Follow the steps in order. Use integer arithmetic exactly as described. Break out of the loop when the proof cannot finish before the horizon.
practice.solution:
def toy_godel(rate0, horizon, candidates, share):
    t = 0
    total = 0
    rate = rate0
    names = []
    for c in candidates:
        name = c[0]
        new_rate = c[1]
        cost = c[2]
        ptime = c[3]
        if t + ptime >= horizon:
            break
        total += ptime * rate * (100 - share) // 100
        t += ptime
        remaining = horizon - t
        stay = remaining * rate * (100 - share) // 100
        if remaining < cost:
            sw = 0
        else:
            sw = (remaining - cost) * new_rate * (100 - share) // 100
        if sw > stay:
            t += cost
            rate = new_rate
            names.append(name)
    total += (horizon - t) * rate * (100 - share) // 100
    return [total, names]
